name: Burmese Way to Socialism
summary: The Burmese Way to Socialism was the state ideology of Burma under Ne Win's Revolutionary Council and the Burma Socialist Programme Party from 1962 to 1988. It combined nationalisation of trade, banking and industry, one-party military-led rule, rejection of Western parliamentary democracy, and an isolationist, Burman-centred nationalism, justified by a mixture of Buddhist, humanist and Marxist ideas that rejected fixed laws of class struggle.
scope: The doctrine as set out in the April 1962 Revolutionary Council policy statement and the 1963 'System of Correlation of Man and His Environment', as put into practice by the BSPP and Ne Win's government through the 1974 constitution. It does not cover the later SLORC and SPDC juntas or the post-1988 market opening. Marxist-style answers are discounted because the text itself distanced the doctrine from Marxism.

sources.title: The Burmese Way to Socialism (Revolutionary Council, 1962), Scribd copy and summary
sources.author: Revolutionary Council of the Union of Burma
sources.usedFor: Only the page summary of the 1962 statement was readable (socialist economy to end exploitation, nationalisation, a peasant and worker led socialist democratic state); the full text was not accessible.

universal-healthcare.rationale: The doctrine promised welfare for peasants and workers through the state, but no source documents a healthcare programme, so a state-guaranteed service is inferred from its statist socialism.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Wages and prices were set centrally by the authorities under the doctrine, so a state-raised wage floor fits its pro-worker rhetoric; no wage-floor policy is documented in the sources.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Nationalising trade, banking and industry in 1963 and banning private industrial investment rejected market allocation outright in favour of state control.

public-ownership.rationale: Oil, mining, banking, trade and large industry were nationalised in 1962-63, which is the core economic act of the doctrine.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: The stated aim of ending exploitation of man by man implies hostility to wealth, but the regime relied on nationalisation and confiscation rather than documented tax policy, so this is inferred.

unions-good.rationale: Independent organisations were suppressed and mass bodies were party-run, so an adherent would not endorse autonomous unions; labour policy is only inferred from the one-party system.

property-fundamental.rationale: Roughly 15,000 firms were taken over and tenancy rents abolished, treating private property as subordinate to the state's socialist programme.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Private corporations were not regulated so much as replaced by state enterprises, but the principle of tight state control over business is central; read here as agreeing.

cut-welfare.rationale: The doctrine presents the state as protector of workers and peasants, so cutting welfare runs against its stated aims; no welfare-specific policy is documented.

worker-ownership.rationale: Ownership was vested in the state, not workers; cooperatives were promoted but accounted for under 2% of factories, so adherents did not clearly back collective worker ownership.

surveillance-ok.rationale: The regime ran a national network of informers and expected citizens to report on one another, so state surveillance was accepted practice.

legalize-drugs.rationale: The doctrine's Buddhist-moral, state-directed outlook suggests opposition to legal recreational drugs; no document addresses it.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: The state tightly censored the press for political reasons, but hate-speech law as such is not documented, and adherents would be split between censorship and nationalist rhetoric.

strong-leader.rationale: Ne Win held the chairmanships of both the Revolutionary Council and the government and ruled by decree, so concentrated leadership above parliamentary gridlock was the practice.

state-harmful.rationale: The doctrine is built on a powerful state and a single leading party; anarchist rejection of the state is the opposite of its position.

limit-guns.rationale: A military regime monopolising force would favour strict civilian arms limits, though this is inferred from its security-state practice.

empower-police-military.rationale: Military officers dominated the party and administration and security councils replaced civil organs, so more authority for the armed forces was central.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: A Buddhist-influenced, nationalist state would be expected to oppose legal prostitution; the sources say nothing on it.

decide-locally.rationale: Control was centralised in Rangoon and the federal system survived in name only, so decentralised decision-making was rejected.

rehabilitation.rationale: No penal philosophy is documented; the regime was repressive yet a Buddhist-humanist doctrine leaves room for rehabilitative language.

traditional-family.rationale: The ideology promoted Burmese culture and Buddhist values, from which a favourable view of traditional family is inferred; it is not stated in the sources.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Nothing documented; a conservative Buddhist-nationalist state would be expected to oppose it.

abortion-legal.rationale: Not addressed; Burmese Buddhist cultural norms and the regime's social conservatism suggest opposition.

more-religion-public.rationale: The doctrine drew on Buddhism and promoted Burmese Buddhism, yet a socialist state kept religion subordinate to the party line; adherents are split.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: The regime's Burmanization policies favoured the majority Burman group and denied Rohingya citizenship, so correcting minority grievances was not a goal.

gender-social-construct.rationale: The doctrine's materialist-humanist language makes it neutral; nothing documented on gender theory.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Eliminating alien influences and promoting a Burmese national identity (Burmanization) was one of the four stated aims of the doctrine.

gradual-change.rationale: The 1962 coup and rapid nationalisation were framed as a revolutionary change after parliamentary democracy failed, so gradual respect for established institutions was rejected.

reduce-immigration.rationale: The regime treated Indians and Chinese as alien, pushing them out of trade and denying Rohingya citizenship, which indicates strong restrictionism.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: The regime was isolationist and expelled foreign agencies, so giving international organisations more power was unlikely.

free-trade.rationale: Trade, foreign and domestic, was nationalised and isolation was deliberate, so free trade was rejected outright.

nation-first.rationale: Isolationism and the drive to put Burma's economy back in Burmese hands made national interest primary over global cooperation.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: A neutralist, isolationist state hostile to foreign interference would reject intervention abroad, which it saw as Western meddling.

open-borders.rationale: Visa restrictions and the expulsion of foreigners from the economy mean open borders contradict the regime's whole approach.

limit-growth.rationale: The regime sought development and industrialisation through a Twenty-Year Plan, so limiting growth for the environment is unlikely; environmental views are inferred.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Not addressed by the doctrine or the sources; no basis to infer a firm position.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: The doctrine emphasised human will and mind over fixed laws, but no stance on technology is documented.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Not addressed; the isolationist state had no nuclear policy documented in sources.

revolution-justified.rationale: The regime itself described the 1962 coup as a revolution and the BSPP as a revolutionary party, so adherents would accept revolutionary change.

experts-over-public.rationale: The regime distrusted foreign experts and relied on military managers, while rejecting popular parliamentary politics; adherents are split.

central-planning.rationale: Production, prices and investment were centrally set through the 1970s, and the 1971 Twenty-Year Plan was the ideal, though the system performed poorly.

socialized-markets.rationale: Markets were tolerated in small business and from 1975 commercial-line guidelines were introduced, but whether public ownership with markets was accepted as principle is unclear.

land-value-tax.rationale: Land was formally state-owned and rents were abolished, but no land-value tax is documented.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Ending exploitation by private wealth implies hostility to inherited fortune, but taxation of inheritance is not stated in the sources.

basic-income.rationale: The regime stressed distribution according to labour contributed, which rules out an unconditional income; this is inferred from the summary of the doctrine.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: The state monopolised foreign trade and sought independent development behind controls; this is protection stronger than tariffs, so agreement is fitting.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Investment levels and production decisions were determined by central authorities well into the 1970s.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Peasants were given de facto land ownership and small industry stayed private, yet big business was nationalised; adherents are not clearly committed to widely spread property as a goal.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: The doctrine envisioned distribution according to labour contributed, which presupposes wages; abolition of money is a communist aim it did not adopt.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Banking was nationalised and state-controlled, so leaving money to the market is the opposite of its approach.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Wages and prices were fixed by the central authorities and mass organisations were party-led, rather than bargaining between employer and worker bodies.

one-party-rule.rationale: All other parties were banned in 1964 and the 1974 constitution made the BSPP the single leading party, a defining feature.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: A revolutionary socialist republic led by army officers rejected hereditary rule; no source reports adherents praising monarchy.

democracy-best.rationale: The Revolutionary Council abolished parliament, saying parliamentary democracy was unsuited to Burma, and called its own state a socialist democracy instead.

direct-votes.rationale: The regime held referendums such as the 1973 constitution vote, yet it rejected competitive politics; direct legislating by citizens is not part of the doctrine.

workers-councils.rationale: Power rested in the party and Revolutionary Council, and workers' bodies were subordinated to them, so councils-not-parliaments was not the model despite worker-peasant rhetoric.

right-to-secede.rationale: The regime centralised control over a nominal federation and resumed military campaigns after 1963 talks failed, so secession was refused.

natural-rulers.rationale: The doctrine's humanist slogan 'Man matters most' is egalitarian, yet the army claimed leadership; adherents are split.

political-violence-never.rationale: The regime used military force against insurgents and protesters and justified it as defence of the revolution; an absolute ban on political violence would not be endorsed.

war-builds-character.rationale: Not documented; isolationist neutralism argues against glorifying war, military culture argues otherwise.

separate-church-state.rationale: Buddhism was part of the ideology's mix but the state also controlled religion; the doctrine did not assert strict separation or union clearly.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: The regime was a secular, socialist military state; it drew on Buddhist ideas but did not base law on scripture.

private-courts-defense.rationale: A state taking over banks and trade and building a security state rejects private provision of courts and defence.

military-superiority.rationale: Neutralist and isolationist, the regime sought strong defence forces but not superiority over rivals; this is inferred.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Burmanization promoted Burman language, culture and Buddhism and the Rohingya were denied citizenship, favouring a nation anchored on the majority group, although the state formally recognised many nationalities.

class-struggle-history.rationale: The 1963 text broke from Marxism, denying fixed laws such as dialectical materialism and stressing human will and mind, and it called communists 'vulgar materialists'.

equal-outcomes.rationale: The goal of ending exploitation and distribution by labour contributed is egalitarian in spirit, but wage and status differences persisted, so agreement is modest and inferred.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Minority regions lost their autonomy to central security councils, so local authority over traditional lands was not recognised.

colonial-reparations.rationale: The ideology was strongly anti-colonial and anti-Western but reparations are not documented as a demand.

civilizational-union.rationale: The regime was isolationist and nationalist, and did not seek political union with other states; inferred.

self-interest-moral.rationale: The doctrine's humanist, anti-exploitation socialism treats private profit-seeking as a social wrong.

duties-before-rights.rationale: A state demanding conformity and suppressing individual freedoms in the name of socialist construction placed collective duty above individual rights, though the formula itself is not quoted.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Buddhist background might support respect for nature, but nothing in the sources treats it as part of the doctrine.

limit-population.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; no basis for a firm position.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: The regime pursued industrialisation as the way to development, so condemning industrial civilisation contradicts its aims.

accelerate-technology.rationale: The regime wanted development but was cautious and isolated, and no source indicates support for disruptive technological acceleration.

human-enhancement.rationale: Not addressed anywhere in the sources.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Anachronistic; the regime favoured human will and its own military managers, so handing decisions to algorithms is inferred as unwelcome.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: A regime that controlled the press and ran informer networks would not allow communications beyond state reach.

restore-past-order.rationale: It saw itself as constructing a new socialist society, though it drew on Burmese tradition; restoring a lost order was not the aim.

results-over-ideology.rationale: The leaders stressed ideology as a guide to action, yet the 1975 commercial-line changes were defended as socialist development; pragmatism was not the declared principle.

direct-action.rationale: The regime took power by coup rather than elections, but it required its own order and banned independent direct action; adherents would not be consistent on this.

means-match-ends.rationale: The regime used authoritarian means (censorship, one-party rule) to build a socialist democracy, which contradicts means matching ends.

return-to-foraging.rationale: The development plans were about industrial and agricultural modernisation, so a hunter-gatherer return is outside the programme.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: The doctrine kept planning, managers and an industrial economy, so it did not seek to abolish the division of labour.

distribute-by-need.rationale: The doctrine specifies distribution according to labour contributed, the lower socialist principle, rather than by need.

production-for-use.rationale: Its aim of replacing exploitation with a planned socialist economy for the people implies production for needs, though the sources give this only in summary.

profit-exploitation.rationale: The doctrine's founding idea is that exploitation of man by man ends only with a socialist economy, implying profit from ownership is exploitative.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: It spoke of peasants and workers as vanguard of a socialist democratic state but rejected Marxist class theory and its 'vulgar materialist' communists; the formula was not adopted.

collective-farming.rationale: The 1963 law gave peasants de facto ownership and agriculture stayed private, with no collectivisation expected.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Anti-Western and anti-imperialist rhetoric exists, yet the doctrine rejected rigid Marxist laws; not documented as a thesis.

taxation-theft.rationale: A state-run socialist economy depends on state revenue and enterprises, so taxation as theft is plainly rejected.

harm-principle.rationale: The regime restricted the press and political activity well beyond preventing harm, so the principle was not accepted.

individual-rights-only.rationale: The doctrine stressed collective and national groups, and 'nationalities' were recognised, so rights belonging only to individuals is rejected; mildly stated.

conscription.rationale: A militarised state would back conscription; no draft policy is documented in the sources, so this is inferred.

exit-over-voice.rationale: The regime restricted foreigners and contact abroad and was hostile to democracy of the Western kind; it would not put exit above voting.

state-as-business.rationale: The state was to own and run enterprises on socialist rather than customer-service lines.

positive-liberty.rationale: The stated aim of ending exploitation implies freedom requires material security, although the sources do not use this idea directly.

media-academia-power.rationale: The regime controlled both press and universities, so the claim does not describe it; no position documented.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Burmanization favoured an ethnic hierarchy in practice, but a doctrine of genetic ability differences is not documented.

organic-representation.rationale: Representation went through party-led mass organisations, not families and trade bodies as such.

total-state.rationale: The state owned the economy, censored media, ran schools and sought to remake values and attitudes, approaching state direction of every area.

national-rebirth.rationale: The coup was presented as a revolution to create a new Burmese national identity after failed parliamentary rule.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Isolationist neutralism; the regime sought no expansion abroad.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Authority rested on a party and army hierarchy, not feudal personal oaths.

bound-labor.rationale: The 1963 law gave peasants land rights and abolished tenancy rents, the reverse of binding farmers to a lord.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: The doctrine claimed a philosophy of man and environment but no position on this epistemic claim is documented.

universal-morality.rationale: Buddhist ethics could support universal morals, but the regime also stressed national specificity; split.

single-common-good.rationale: The ideology proposed one planned socialist path for the people rather than competing interests; this is inferred from its anti-party-politics stance.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: Nothing in the doctrine concerns this; the state was neutralist.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: The regime stripped citizenship from or excluded those it viewed as foreign; a broad diaspora right of return is unlikely.

revive-national-language.rationale: English teaching was cut back and Burmese promoted; revival of a lapsed language is not the case, so agreement is a weak inference from the language policy.

workplace-democracy.rationale: In 1975 management committees took over production decisions, but control stayed with the party-state, not workers; unclear.

school-vouchers.rationale: The state ran education and sought to shape attitudes, so public vouchers for private choice conflict with it.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: No fiscal doctrine is documented; the regime ran growing foreign debt.

economic-freedom.rationale: The regime curtailed private enterprise while stifling politics too, and it did not believe political freedom depends on economic freedom.

rule-by-example.rationale: The regime relied on censorship, informers and security councils rather than moral example.

national-self-determination.rationale: The regime's anti-colonial framing supports the principle for Burma, but it denied it to minorities inside Burma, so agreement is moderate.

force-without-un.rationale: Neutralism and isolationism meant no foreign use of force; inferred.

reason-over-faith.rationale: The doctrine mixed Buddhist metaphysics with materialist ideas, and the leadership kept faith in astrology, so reason as the only guide was not its view.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: With non-Burmans treated as alien, reserving state benefits for citizens is likely; no welfare rules are documented.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Distribution by labour contributed supports work-based reward, but no welfare condition is documented.

class-collaboration.rationale: The doctrine denied fixed laws of class struggle and spoke of workers and peasants together as the base of one socialist state, but it also attacked exploiters; adherents are not clearly for employer-worker partnership.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: The ideology prized Burmese culture and Buddhism, so sacrificing inherited institutions is rejected.

dominated-front.rationale: The regime was anti-Western and non-aligned, so it would sympathise with dominated-country cooperation, but it avoided alliances.

workers-nation.rationale: The regime made class subordinate to national unity and Burmanization, rejecting international class organisation.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: The sources record no gender-role policy for the doctrine, so no position can be stated.

ban-interest.rationale: State banking, not a religious ban on interest, was the policy; no sources show a prohibition.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Citizenship denied the Rohingya and ethnic Chinese and Indians were pushed out of trade, but no law of residential racial segregation is documented.

state-class-instrument.rationale: The doctrine rejected Marxist theory and presented its own state as serving all workers and peasants, not as an instrument of a ruling class.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Oil and mining were nationalised under the state Burma Oil Company and offshore drilling was prioritised in the 1970s.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Burmanization pushed Burman language, culture and Buddhism on others and residents of foreign descent were treated as aliens.

elite-replacement.rationale: Not documented as a belief, though xenophobic suspicion of foreign blood was voiced; not a core claim.

proportional-representation.rationale: The one-party assembly elections were uncontested, so multi-party proportional allocation was not its model.

national-mission.rationale: Isolationism implies no mission to export its model.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: The doctrine's class and nationality analysis says nothing about structural patriarchy, so no position is documented.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: The doctrine blamed the politicians of parliamentary democracy for deviating from socialist aims; later the regime itself was corrupt but adherents would still voice this for the earlier rulers.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: No eugenic policy is documented in the sources.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: The army and police dominated the state and answered to no civilian courts that the regime had altered.

night-watchman-state.rationale: A state owning the economy and directing development is the opposite of a minimal state.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Policies on citizenship and 'pure Burmese' status are reported, but no stance on discouraging marriage is documented.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The doctrine's humanist slogan 'Man matters most' affirms human worth in principle, though minority citizenship was unequal in practice, so moderate agreement.

socialism-one-country.rationale: The regime pursued an isolationist national road with no revolutionary internationalism.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Not documented; Buddhist-majority state but no stated stance.

restrict-conversion.rationale: The regime promoted Burmese Buddhism but no conversion law is documented.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Not documented; Theravada tradition does not require it.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Not documented; Buddhist influence versus socialist secularism cuts both ways.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: The state saw itself as vigilant against foreign influence and insurgents, but the Marxist 'encirclement' argument is not used in the sources.

consent-of-governed.rationale: The regime claimed a socialist democracy but its authority rested on a coup; formal consent doctrine is not stated.

trade-surplus.rationale: Not documented as a goal; state trade control sought independence.

population-transfer.rationale: Expelling or pressuring minorities occurred in practice (Indians and Chinese left, Rohingya excluded), but as an endorsed principle it is not documented.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: The state seized private property by nationalisation and enforced it with force.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: A doctrine opposing exploitation and capitalism and stressing cooperation rejects competition as the engine.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: The regime banned all parties in 1964 and seized their assets, so outlawing hostile parties was normal practice.

separated-powers.rationale: The Revolutionary Council held legislative and executive power, courts were changed, and power was centralised in the party and army.

vanguard-party.rationale: The BSPP was modelled on a Marxist-Leninist cadre party, but the doctrine calls itself nationalist rather than speaking of workers' revolutionary consciousness; moderate agreement.

priority-to-poor.rationale: The doctrine presents peasants and workers as the base of a socialist democratic state, so laws favouring them are its stated aim.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Independent unions and protests were suppressed, so a law restricting strikes would be accepted, though not by secret-ballot rules specifically.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: The doctrine ascribed poverty to exploitation and colonial economics rather than population; inferred.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Burmanization was intended to build national unity by promoting one culture, treating ethnic diversity as a cohesion problem.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Offices were filled by party and army appointees, so a lottery is alien to the system.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Constitutional protections were suspended where Revolutionary Council decrees applied, framed as necessary to protect the revolution.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Prices were fixed by central authorities and the state controlled distribution, so maximum prices follow naturally.

party-controls-media.rationale: The free press was outlawed, the Working People's Daily replaced it and the state news agency replaced foreign agencies.

party-commands-army.rationale: The party was dominated by the military rather than controlling it; over half of party members were soldiers or police, so the party-over-army principle is unsettled.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: The regime was restrictive on citizenship, denying it to Rohingya; length of residence rules are not specified.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: No rule on officials' pay is documented in the sources on the doctrine.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: The BSPP was a Leninist-style cadre party, so binding discipline on members is consistent; the exact rule is inferred.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Isolationism and nationalism rule out pooling sovereignty.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Ne Win as chairman of the Council and government commanded the army, so concentrated command under the head suits the model.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Not applicable to the Buddhist context; no position.

clerical-rule.rationale: The state was run by military officers and a socialist party, and monks were among protesters it repressed.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Not documented; a nationalist neutral state would not advocate defeating its own government.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: A press scrutiny regime was created and censorship was normal; moral grounds for art censorship are inferred.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Ne Win served as party chairman for decades, and the party was the sole legal one, so term limits were not part of its design.

recall-officials.rationale: Officials were party appointees; recall by voters is not part of the system.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Neutralist isolationism meant Burma avoided alliances and foreign bases; adherents would support ending permanent alliances.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: No housing tenure policy is documented for the doctrine.

people-in-arms.rationale: The army was the core institution of the regime and its leaders were professional officers, so replacing it with an armed citizenry is rejected.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Peasants were called a vanguard of the state, but no moral claim about rural life is documented.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: The doctrine concerned Burma alone and never raised a divided-nation claim.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: The regime was hostile to the university milieu (it blew up the Student Union building in 1962) but made no documented claim of this kind.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Burmanization elevated Burman culture and Buddhism over others, though formal rhetoric recognised many nationalities.

death-penalty.rationale: A security state facing insurgency would retain capital punishment; not specifically documented.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Not addressed; a conservative state-run schooling system is inferred.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: The doctrine claimed a scientific-sounding philosophy of man and environment; creationism is not part of Theravada state policy.

restrict-pornography.rationale: A censoring state with a Buddhist-moral outlook would restrict it; inferred from press censorship.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Rohingya were denied citizenship despite birth in the territory and 'pure Burmese' descent was prized, which fits descent-based citizenship.

minority-language-support.rationale: Burmanization promoted Burmese language and culture through schools and media at minority expense.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Not documented; the regime's religious policy favoured Buddhism and uniform control.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: The state expected conformity and censored dissent.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Burma accumulated about 4.9 billion dollars of foreign debt and sought aid late in the period; no demand to cancel debts is documented.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Nationalisation was meant to put the economy back in Burmese hands from foreign and minority control to assert independence.

constituent-assembly.rationale: The 1974 constitution was approved by referendum, but the 1947 constitution was swept away by a coup, so an elected constituent assembly was not the method.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: The regime curtailed political freedoms and defended its approach as socialist development, so adherents would accept temporary limits.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: The regime refused non-governmental aid and expelled foreign agencies while later asking for multilateral aid; adherents were split.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Not addressed; neutralism makes it unlikely.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: The head of state was chosen through the party-controlled assembly after 1974; not a doctrine matter.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Banking was nationalised and the currency demonetised by the government, so independence from the executive was rejected.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Peace talks with minority insurgents failed in 1963 and the army fought on, but no explicit territorial position is documented.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Private property was permitted only where it served the state's socialist programme, with large holdings nationalised and tenancy abolished.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: The regime sought Eastern European-style socialism, so it was unlikely to call the USSR state capitalist.

collective-defense.rationale: Isolationism and neutralism mean it avoided collective defence commitments.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: The state was the supreme institution and later controlled the Buddhist sangha, but this is inferred, not documented in the sources used.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: The head of state was also leader of the sole ruling party, so a nonpartisan symbolic head was not its model.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Military campaigns against ethnic insurgents resumed after 1963 talks failed, and the Four Cuts followed.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Federal arrangements were kept in name only and replaced by central security councils.

sacred-ruler.rationale: A republican socialist military regime would not claim a sacred ruler.

flat-income-tax.rationale: The doctrine's egalitarian aims suggest progressive rather than flat taxation; taxation is not specified in the sources.

character-from-environment.rationale: The 1963 'Correlation of Man and His Environment' text treats man as shaped by and acting on his environment, with social conditions mattering.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Ne Win ruled by decree and the courts were changed, but the doctrine did not state that the ruler is above law.

space-expansion.rationale: Not addressed; isolationist development priorities suggest low interest.

mixed-constitution.rationale: A single-party structure is not mixed rule.

leader-cult.rationale: Ne Win cultivated an image as national hero, but no formal public cult is documented in the sources.

equal-parenting.rationale: Family law and custody rules are not addressed in the doctrine or the sources.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: The doctrine denied fixed laws of class struggle and the party saw itself as representing all working people.

land-redistribution.rationale: The 1963 law and the abolition of tenancy rents in 1965 transferred land rights from landlords to cultivators.

refugee-return.rationale: Rohingya were denied citizenship and Indians and Chinese were pushed out, so a return right is unlikely.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: The regime was inward-looking; no irredentist claim is documented.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Not addressed; the state was not a religious state.

women-must-cover.rationale: No such Buddhist or socialist rule is documented.

common-currency.rationale: The regime stressed national control of money, including demonetisation, so a shared foreign currency would be rejected.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Not addressed; the doctrine's nationalism is Burma-focused.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: The federal system survived in name only and cultural policy was Burmanizing.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: The 1963 text rejected dialectical materialism and put weight on human will and cultivation of mind.

ban-cartels.rationale: The state replaced private monopolies with state ones; breaking up private concentrations is consistent, though the stated method was nationalisation.

no-bailouts.rationale: Failing state enterprises were subsidised until the 1975 guidelines; private firm bailouts are not applicable.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Courts were reshaped by the regime and bound to its program, but the 'majority' framing does not fit a one-party state.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: The state sought independent development and maximal control over trade to isolate the economy from outside influence.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Trade agreements were rejected broadly; this specific standard is not addressed.

moral-incentives.rationale: Moral incentives were stressed until 1975, then the 1975 guidelines introduced bonuses and 'material' incentives that the leadership defended as socialist; adherents therefore split.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: The Revolutionary Council was an army group that carried out the 1962 coup and called it a revolution.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: A revolutionary socialist republic opposed landlords' and feudal privileges, though hereditary titles are not directly mentioned.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Burmanization promoted Burmese language and culture in schools and media.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: The doctrine is strongly anti-colonial and anti-Western.

patriotic-education.rationale: Schools promoted a national identity and Burmese culture, so pupils were taught national pride; no flag-specific policy is documented.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Not documented; Burmese policy favoured the majority group, but not through admissions preferences.

public-money-creation.rationale: The state controlled all banking and currency, which fits public money creation, though it is not described as a policy principle.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: The doctrine considered capitalism exploitative and doomed for Burma, though it rejected deterministic Marxist laws, so only mildly.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Isolationism and anti-colonialism rule out a policy of cultivating influence.

delink-world-market.rationale: Isolationism, expulsion of foreign agencies and state trade monopoly delinked Burma from rich-country markets.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: The doctrine was not framed around a theory of rich-country workers' exploitation, so no position is documented.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: The state controlled the economy and sought national unity; the doctrine rejects private owners' absolute freedom.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Constitutional protections were suspended by decree and courts reshaped, so limits on government were resisted.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: The sources record no stance on colonial-era treaties in the doctrine.

elective-rulers.rationale: Not relevant to a republican one-party state; the choice was by party-controlled processes.

minority-veto.rationale: Dissent was suppressed and decisions bound everyone under party discipline.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Protest and opposition were repressed, so resisting the ruler was not accepted.

parliament-supreme.rationale: The Revolutionary Council replaced parliament and argued that parliamentary democracy failed, so parliamentary supremacy was rejected.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Buddhist background favours compassion for animals but the doctrine is silent; split.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Animal use is not addressed in the doctrine or in the sources.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: The doctrine ended private wealth by nationalisation, so reliance on voluntary duty of the rich is not its model.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: The regime required mass membership and obliged students to join the Programme Youth Organisation.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: No cultural-critique thesis of this kind appears in the doctrine or the sources.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: Not documented; the regime used coercion and informers rather than a consent-through-culture theory.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Foreign advisers were distrusted and nationalisation sought to end foreign domination of the economy, consistent with a view of extraction.

native-born-offices.rationale: Policy promoted 'pure Burmese' participation and treated foreign-blooded residents as outsiders, so offices for native-born citizens fits.

party-own-road.rationale: The doctrine is by name a distinctively Burmese road to socialism and rejects dependence on Marxist or Soviet models.

return-lost-territory.rationale: The doctrine made no claims on territory lost to neighbours.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Burmanization gave political primacy to the Burman majority, a loose analogue; the principle for pre-colonial peoples is not stated.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Not addressed; the army was founded with Japanese help and later fought the Japanese.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: The regime saw itself as socialist and called communists vulgar materialists, but no document speaks of this equivalence.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Not documented; the regime destroyed the Student Union building but this is a different matter.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: Gendered disadvantage in education or health is not addressed by the doctrine.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: Domestic violence policy is not addressed by the doctrine or the sources.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: The 1962 statement held that Western-style parliamentary democracy did not suit Burma and called for a socialist democracy on Burmese lines.

military-guardian-role.rationale: The army seized power in 1962 and dominated the party and the state, justifying itself as guardian of the nation.

paid-care-work.rationale: The doctrine's wage-by-labour principle is silent on unpaid domestic work, and the sources give no policy.

filial-duty.rationale: Buddhist-Burmese tradition emphasises filial respect, but the doctrine does not address it; inferred.

office-by-exam.rationale: Posts went to party and army loyalists; exams not addressed.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Foreign capital was excluded for decades, and even later joint ventures stayed under state enterprise ownership.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Divorce law is not addressed by the doctrine or the sources.

recallable-delegates.rationale: The party hierarchy appointed officials; recall by those who chose them was not its design.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: A nationalised banking system and state-run economy leave no room for private pension funds.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Land was formally state-owned and peasants held it by use rights under the 1963 law.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Parliament was abolished and the Council ran finances by decree.

single-official-language.rationale: Burmanization elevated Burmese in schools and media while English teaching was cut back.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: The economy was returned to Burmese hands and foreign influence barred, so foreign land ownership was unacceptable.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: Not addressed; Burmanization itself produced disparities.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: The doctrine's Buddhist-socialist character and rejection of the capitalist market imply scepticism of consumerism; inferred.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Isolationist neutralism rules out arming foreign insurgents.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Non-aligned neutralism means it would not support intervention in allied states.

corporate-influence.rationale: Foreign and private capital were treated as hostile influences; inferred.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: Foreign agencies such as the Ford Foundation and Asia Foundation were expelled and only government-to-government aid was allowed.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Population and family-incentive policy is not addressed in the sources on the doctrine.

residents-only-property.rationale: Not addressed; land belonged to the state.

job-guarantee.rationale: As a state-run economy built to serve workers, guaranteed employment fits the model but no jobs guarantee is documented.

democratic-peace.rationale: The doctrine rejected Western democratic models, so the thesis would not appeal.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: The regime demanded obedience and punished dissent.

non-intervention.rationale: Isolationism and neutralism assert strict non-interference by foreigners in Burma's affairs.

industrial-unions.rationale: No trade-union structure beyond party-led mass organisations is documented.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Scapegoating of Chinese minority is reported after 1967 riots, but conspiracy theory is not a doctrine.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Not part of Buddhist-socialist programme and not a leftist radical aim of this regime.

public-access-to-information.rationale: The regime censored the press, created the Press Scrutiny Board and replaced foreign agencies with a state news agency.

local-production.rationale: Self-sufficiency and import substitution were aims, though local production for local consumption is inferred.

informal-organisation.rationale: The regime banned other parties and ran mass organisations under party control.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Isolationism and sovereignty emphasis imply domestic law outranks international law.

religious-nation.rationale: The state promoted Buddhism culturally but officially recognised many nationalities, so defining the nation by religion was not formal doctrine.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Foreign aid agencies were expelled, only government-to-government aid was accepted, and the leadership distrusted foreign advisers, stressing independent Burmese development.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Inferred from its isolationist, sovereignty-first nationalism, which kept Burma out of blocs and rejected foreign tutelage.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: The 1962 coup ended the Shan and ethnic federal movements and centralised the state, so regional retention of revenue is inferred as rejected.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Inferred from a doctrine that nationalised industry, banking and trade while leaving personal property and small holdings to individuals.

defeat-communism.rationale: The BSPP fought the Communist Party insurgency and rejected Marxist class-struggle laws, so defeating communism is inferred, though it claimed neutrality abroad.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Trade, banking, industry and key services were nationalised in 1963, leaving little role for private or independent providers.

religion-illusion.rationale: The doctrine's humanism was materialist and distanced from religion as a guide to policy, though the state courted Buddhism, so an illusion-fading view is inferred.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: The Burmese Way treated capitalism as exploitative and nationalised private enterprise, rejecting it as a basis for a better society.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: Inferred from its socialist egalitarianism and state-led worker welfare; women's issues are not documented as a focus.

socialized-care.rationale: Inferred: the state promised welfare for workers but no source describes socialised housework or childcare, and the doctrine was socially traditional.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Inferred from Burmanization, which privileged Burmese language and culture over foreign influence; no loanword programme is sourced.

treaties-binding.rationale: The regime abolished the federal arrangements of the Panglong-era union constitution by decree, implying treaties with ethnic nationalities were not binding.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Cooperatives were promoted as part of the socialist economy, though under state direction rather than as self-governing communes.

majority-settlement.rationale: Inferred from Burmanization, which favoured the Burman majority and moved Burmese administration and settlement into minority areas.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: The doctrine presented itself as a distinct Burmese path that rejected both Western parliamentary capitalism and Marxist orthodoxy.

historical-land-claim.rationale: The doctrine stressed Burman-centred nationalism but the sources record no historical or religious land claim as a principle.

holocaust-denial.rationale: Not addressed by the sources; inferred as rejection, since the doctrine had no connection to such claims.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Colonial-era criminal law on homosexuality stayed in force and the regime was socially conservative; the sources do not address it directly.

suppress-opposition.rationale: The BSPP was the only legal party under the one-party system and the military-led regime rejected parliamentary opposition.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: The regime kept religion under state control and justified itself by humanist as well as Buddhist ideas, so punishing blasphemy is inferred as not a priority.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: The doctrine grew out of anti-colonial nationalism and rejected foreign economic domination, so exploiting colonies is inferred as opposed.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: The doctrine says nothing on Muslim jihad; the question is outside its concerns.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: The doctrine was run by a secular military and rejected religious rule of the state; inferred.

participatory-democracy.rationale: The doctrine rejected Western parliamentary democracy and ran things through party and army, though it later set up people's councils; inferred.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: The doctrine framed class struggle as non-fixed and nation-focused; intersectional analysis is inferred as absent.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the regime's conservative social outlook.

assisted-dying.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from Buddhist-influenced and conservative social norms.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: The doctrine claimed to be neither capitalist nor orthodox Marxist, but it was a state socialism in practice; split reading.

alienated-labor.rationale: The text distanced itself from Marxism and its theory of class struggle, so adherents would not clearly adopt this Marxist claim.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Not addressed by the sources; Burman-centred nationalism distrusted Muslims but the claim about Western countries is outside it.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: The regime justified itself by humanist and Marxist-influenced ideas rather than divine authority; inferred.

ban-nda-harassment.rationale: Not addressed in the sources and unrelated to the doctrine.

social-market-economy.rationale: The doctrine nationalised trade, banking and industry and rejected free markets, so a social-market blend is not its model.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: The regime was military-led and built on the army, so abolishing armed forces is contrary to it.

rich-first.rationale: The doctrine pursued state-led egalitarian socialism and nationalised wealth; inferred that letting some get rich first was rejected.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: The regime pursued isolationism and stayed out of blocs, a posture documented in the sources.

dynastic-succession.rationale: The BSPP ran a one-party socialist republic opposed to feudal and hereditary privilege, and nothing in the sources suggests leaders could pass office to children.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: Banks were nationalised and run by the state, not owned by their users, so user-owned mutual credit does not fit; inferred from the ownership pattern.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: The regime pursued isolationism and self-reliance and shut out foreign influence, so it would refuse conditions imposed from abroad.

property-franchise.rationale: The regime claimed to be led by peasants and workers and ruled through the army and party, so a property qualification is the opposite of its stated basis; inferred.

domination-women-nature.rationale: The doctrine does not address feminism or ecology.

reification.rationale: The doctrine distanced itself from Marxism, so this Marxist concept is not part of it and adherents have no clear position.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: The press was brought under state control and the doctrine aimed to end exploitation by the wealthy, so ownership of the press by private wealth was rejected.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: The Revolutionary Council suspended the constitution and ruled by decree through security councils, which contradicts rule only by standing laws.

racial-franchise.rationale: The regime was Burman-centred and excluded Chinese and Indian minorities economically, but its constitution framed the state around class, not a racial franchise; inferred.

online-participation.rationale: The regime tightly controlled information and communication, so open online deliberation would not fit; anachronistic and inferred.

open-government-data.rationale: The regime was secretive and controlled the press, and decisions were made by the army and party without public records.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: The doctrine did not address marriage law, and the later Buddhist-nationalist marriage laws belong to a different period.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: State nationalisation of trade removed Indian and Chinese shops, but this was state action rather than consumer boycott, which a one-party state would not encourage; inferred.

citizens-assembly.rationale: Deliberation by randomly selected citizens does not fit a one-party, army-led state which appointed its councils.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: The doctrine mixed Buddhist, humanist and Marxist ideas and reworked Buddhism to fit socialism, so reinterpretation for modern conditions is inferred.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Inferred from its state socialism and nationalisation of industry and trade, which aimed to break concentrated private wealth; liberty framing is not in the sources.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Inferred from the conservative, military-led character of the regime; no source documents policy on open service.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: The doctrine rejected Marxist dogma and the regime kept state ties to Buddhism, so state-promoted atheism is unlikely; inferred, not documented.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Inferred from a military-led one-party state that relied on police and prisons to maintain order; abolition is not discussed.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: Inferred from the regime favouring a Burman-centred unitary state over ethnic power-sharing, as the sources describe its nationalism.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Inferred from its nationalisation of trade and banking and its view that the state should provide for peasants and workers.

term-limits.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; the BSPP ran a one-party system with no electoral competition to limit.

vote-delegation.rationale: Inferred from one-party military rule that rejected Western parliamentary democracy; delegable voting was not on offer.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: Inferred from a state focused on immediate national economic problems; no source addresses extinction risk.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Not addressed in the sources, and the regime proclaimed equality of the sexes while leaving religious bodies largely to themselves.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; the doctrine did not set out family law positions.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: The regime pushed out Chinese and Indian residents and treated non-Burmans as outsiders, so extending local votes to foreigners is inferred to be unwelcome.

rent-control.rationale: A state that nationalised trade and planned the economy would readily fix rents by law; inferred from its command-economy approach, not a documented housing policy.

abolish-ip.rationale: The doctrine never addressed patents or copyright, and a closed state economy gives no clear lean either way.

uniformed-youth.rationale: The BSPP ran mass organisations and the army-led state sought to mobilise youth for national tasks; inferred from its one-party mass-organisation model.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: Its isolationist neutralism implies no great-power weapons on Burmese soil; inferred, as the doctrine never mentioned nuclear arms.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: The regime's isolationism and insistence on self-reliance left no room for foreign bases on Burmese soil.

recognise-genocide.rationale: The regime's Burman-centred nationalism and treatment of minorities make it unlikely to endorse formal recognition of past persecutions; inferred.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: The 1962 statement's aim was a socialist economy to end exploitation, with income going to workers and peasants rather than owners.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Buddhist humanist ethics oppose killing, but the military-led regime itself used force freely; adherents' stated ethics lean to the answer, inferred.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Burman nationalism presented the nation as continuous with its pre-colonial kingdoms; inferred from the regime's nationalist emphasis.

sex-socially-constructed.rationale: Not a concern of the doctrine; its humanist-Buddhist materialism and conservative social order lean against this claim, inferred.

no-fixed-category-of-women.rationale: Feminist theory was outside the doctrine; the one-party state's class framing leaves no room for it, inferred.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: A military regime that celebrated national heroes, and Burmese nationalism honours those who died for independence; inferred.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: The doctrine was a humanist, materialist-leaning programme that kept religion separate from politics; inferred.

homeland-cultural-centre.rationale: Its nationalism sought to keep all Burmans within the state and hostile to diaspora Indians and Chinese; inferred.

culture-before-state.rationale: The regime put state-building and control of the state first, with culture serving the state; inferred.

god-not-male.rationale: Theravada Buddhism has no creator God, and the doctrine did not address the question.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: Not addressed; the regime's conservative social order and indifference to gender questions make agreement unlikely, inferred.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: Burmanization of the economy nationalised trade and industry to remove Chinese, Indian and foreign business owners.

single-unit-for-people.rationale: The regime kept a centralised unitary state and resisted ethnic autonomy demands; inferred.

independent-unions.rationale: The BSPP ran workers' and peasants' organisations as party bodies under state control.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: The doctrine rejected Marxist class doctrine and put power in a military-led party, so state ownership counted as socialism.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Industry, trade and banking were nationalised, so basic services fit state ownership; no source covers local services specifically.

second-chamber.rationale: Under the 1974 constitution power sat in a single chamber, the Pyithu Hluttaw, under the one-party system.

municipal-property.rationale: Nationalisation put productive assets under the state, not local communities.

confederal-coordination.rationale: The doctrine was centralist and one-party, with no confederal local assemblies.

faster-drug-approval.rationale: State-run, cautious and isolationist administration; inferred.

ageing-research-funding.rationale: No source shows interest in such research; inferred from isolationist state planning.

anonymous-payments.rationale: The state controlled banking and demonetised notes without warning, so untraceable payments were opposed.

online-anonymity.rationale: A tightly controlled state with censorship; inferred.

person-over-state.rationale: The state and party set the ends and the individual served the socialist programme; inferred.

spiritual-nature.rationale: The doctrine drew on Buddhist and humanist ideas alongside material aims.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: The state was unitary and centralised, with nominal ethnic states under central control.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Ethnic minority politics was suppressed in favour of unified national socialism; inferred.

racial-pride.rationale: Burman-centred nationalism favoured pride in national heritage; inferred.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Isolationist neutrality suggests force for defence; inferred.

missingStatements.text: Retail and wholesale trade should be run by the state rather than by private merchants.
missingStatements.rationale: All domestic and foreign trade was nationalised in 1963, which was reported as the most far-reaching of the nationalisations and tied to Burmanization.

notes: The primary text on burmalibrary.org returned 403 to every fetch, so the 1962 statement is documented here through scholarly summaries and a Scribd summary. Many answers on social and cultural issues are low-confidence inferences, since the doctrine focused on economy, state structure and nationalism. The regime's practice (for example the 1975 commercial guidelines, later foreign investment) departed from its stated doctrine.
